info.text: How phonology turns raw sound into a system: the phoneme as a language's unit of contrast, the allophones it varies through, and the syllable patterns and melodic layers that organize them.

clusters.name: The phoneme & its variants
clusters.fact: The machinery by which a language sorts continuously varying sounds into a small set of meaning-distinguishing categories.

allophone.text: A context-determined variant of a phoneme whose substitution never changes meaning: English [pʰ] in 'pot' and [p] in 'spot' are allophones of /p/.

complementary distribution.text: Two related sounds never occur in the same environment — English aspirated [pʰ] only syllable-initially, plain [p] elsewhere — so the position selects the variant.

free variation.text: Two sounds occur in the same environment without changing meaning; the choice follows the speaker or habit, as with released versus unreleased final stops.

minimal pair.text: Two words identical except for one sound with different meanings — 'ship' versus 'sheep' — the standard evidence that two sounds are separate phonemes.

phone.text: Any actual speech sound produced, written in square brackets: [pʰ] and [p] are two distinct phones.

phoneme.text: A family of sounds speakers treat as one unit; swapping it for a different phoneme changes word meaning — /p/ versus /b/ in 'pat'/'bat'.

clusters.name: Syllable & position
clusters.fact: How a language strings sounds into syllables with named parts — and the positional rules about which sounds may go where.

coda.text: The consonant or consonants after the syllable's vowel — the /k/ at the end of 'sock'. English phonotactics forbids /h/ and /ŋ/ from certain positions: /ŋ/ occurs only in the coda.

onset.text: The consonant or cluster before the syllable's vowel — the /t/ in 'tea' or /str/ in 'string'.

phonotactics.text: A language's positional rules for sound sequences: English allows 'str-' to open a word but never /ŋ/, which appears only at syllable ends.

rime.text: The vowel plus any closing consonants — the part that rhymes: /aɪt/ in 'light' and 'night'.

syllable structure.text: The organization of speech into syllables with a vowel nucleus and consonal margins — the beats stress and timing count.

clusters.name: Stress, tone & intonation
clusters.fact: Meaning-bearing melody layered over the string of segments: loudness, pitch, and tune doing grammatical and attitudinal work.

intonation.text: The tune of a whole utterance — rising in questions, falling in statements — carrying sentence mood and attitude rather than word identity.

stress.text: Relative prominence on one syllable, contrastive in English: 'PERmit' (noun) versus 'perMIT' (verb).

tone.text: Contrastive pitch on a syllable that distinguishes words — Mandarin mā 'mother' versus mà 'scold' differ only in pitch.

bridges.fact: Both complementary distribution and phonotactics are positional claims: English /ŋ/ (as in 'sing') never begins a syllable, so where a sound may occur is what selects it.

info.text: Where a sound may occur is a fact about the language's system, not the vocal tract: complementary distribution states it for one phoneme's variants; phonotactics states it for the whole language.

bridges.fact: Stress and tone distinguish words exactly as consonants and vowels do — English reCORD (verb) vs RECord (noun), Mandarin mā 'mother' vs mà 'scold'.

info.text: The phoneme principle — swap this, change the meaning — holds for pitch and loudness too, not just consonants and vowels.

bridges.fact: Stress and tone attach to syllables, not segments: English stress picks one syllable of a word, and the vowels of unstressed syllables reduce toward schwa.

info.text: Melody rides on syllables: stress chooses among a word's syllables, tone rides each syllable's vowel, and the unstressed ones are where vowels reduce to schwa.

lenses.prompt: Which terms describe relationships in which swapping one sound for another never changes a word's meaning?
lenses.explanation: In all three relationships, substituting one sound for the other never changes a word's meaning: allophones are a phoneme's context-determined variants, complementary distribution places them where the other never occurs, and free variation lets either appear unpredictably. A minimal pair is the opposite — the one swap that does change meaning — and phone names a single produced sound, not a relationship.

lenses.prompt: Which melodic terms distinguish individual words rather than shaping whole utterances?
lenses.explanation: Stress distinguishes words from one another ('PERmit' vs 'perMIT') and tone distinguishes words in Mandarin (mā vs mà). Intonation is different: it is the tune of a whole utterance — questions rise, statements fall — and does not distinguish individual words.

lenses.prompt: Which terms name positions within a syllable?
lenses.explanation: Onset, rime, and coda are the named positions within a syllable: onset before the vowel, rime as the vowel-plus-coda rhyming part, coda after the vowel. Syllable structure names the whole organization, and phonotactics states which sounds may fill which sequences — rules, not positions.

lenses.prompt: Which terms are statements about where a sound may occur?
lenses.explanation: Both are claims about where a sound may occur: complementary distribution is that claim made about one phoneme's variants (English [pʰ] only syllable-initially, plain [p] elsewhere), and phonotactics is the same kind of claim at the language level (/ŋ/ never begins a syllable). Free variation is the opposite — no positional rule at all — and onset and coda are positions themselves, not claims about them.

entries.reason: Play first: the contrasts organized on this board are built from the consonants and vowels described in Consonants and Vowels.

learningIntroduction.title: From Sound to System
learningIntroduction.summary: How languages sort raw sound into contrast: the phoneme and its allophones, the syllable templates that position sounds, and the melodic layers of stress, tone, and intonation.

content.text:
The previous lesson described speech sounds as physical gestures — place, manner, voicing, vowel dimensions. This lesson asks a different question: which of the infinitely many possible sound differences does a language actually treat as meaningful? English ignores the puff of air after the p in 'pot'; Thai builds word meanings on exactly that puff. Each language sorts the continuous stream of sound into a small inventory of contrastive categories, and each category is a **phoneme**.

Any actual sound a speaker produces is a **phone**. English speakers treat [pʰ] of 'pot' and plain [p] of 'spot' as the same thing — the phoneme /p/ — and its two contextual variants are **allophones**. How do linguists discover a language's phonemes? Two tools do most of the work. A **minimal pair** — two words identical except for one sound, like 'ship' and 'sheep' — proves the two sounds are separate phonemes, because swapping them changes the meaning. And when no meaning ever changes, the sounds belong to one phoneme: English [pʰ] and [p] stand in **complementary distribution**, each appearing only where the other never does. When either sound may occur in the same spot with no change in meaning, the choice is **free variation**, down to the individual speaker. Crucially, the sorting differs by language: [n] and [ŋ] are separate phonemes in English ('sin' vs 'sing') but variants of one phoneme in Spanish, while aspiration is a full phoneme in Thai.

Sounds are also positioned. **Syllable structure** gives every utterance a rhythm of beats: each syllable has an **onset** (its opening consonant or cluster), a vowel nucleus, and optionally a **coda** (its closing consonant); the vowel-plus-coda part is the **rime**, the part that rhymes. On top of the template sit **phonotactics**, a language's positional rules: English allows 'str-' to open a word but never /ŋ/, which appears only in the coda, as in 'sing'. Where a sound may occur is a fact about the language's system, not about the human vocal tract.

Finally, melody rides above the segments. **Stress** makes one syllable of a word more prominent, and in English that choice alone distinguishes nouns from verbs — 'PERmit' versus 'perMIT'. **Tone** gives each syllable a contrastive pitch, so Mandarin mā ('mother') and mà ('scold') differ only in melody. **Intonation** is the tune of a whole utterance, rising in questions and falling in statements. Stress and tone do for melody exactly what phonemes do for segments: swapping them changes what a word means.

Together, the two lessons give the full picture of the sound level of language: how speech sounds are produced, and how each language organizes them into the contrasts and patterns that carry meaning.
